text.text: Run the shop from here. Walk-ins and bookings land on the Cuts board; each finished cut records the price, tip and how long the client waited. Client cards say how each regular likes it and who their barber is. Commission barbers are paid from the cuts; renters pay weekly in Chair rent. Members pay monthly in Payments.

pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the shop runs in this workspace. Share it with every barber and the front desk.
What lives where
Services and memberships
: each cut and shave with price and time, the monthly membership, and how many of each you did.
Clients
: usual cut, usual barber, how they like it, visits, no-shows and spend.
Cuts
: every walk-in and booking, with barber, price, tip and wait time.
Payments
: card, cash and tap payments, and monthly membership charges.
Chair rent
: weekly rent from barbers who rent their chair.
A cut from door to paid
Booked clients are on the Cuts calendar; walk-ins are added at the door as
Walk-in
When the client sits down, record how long they waited.
After the cut, press
Mark done
, add the tip, and take payment (
Mark paid
Members' cuts carry no price; their monthly payment covers them.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, today's bookings, failed member payments
Every Monday: chair rent for the week, commission for last week
Every month: walk-in share and waits, membership numbers
Making it yours

Change services and prices to your own, set your commission and rent amounts, and delete the sample clients once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Regulars are the business
Most of a shop's income comes from regulars who come back every two to four weeks. Write how they like it on their card after the first cut, and the next barber gets it right without asking twice.
Tips and no-shows
Tips belong to the barber in full; record them on the cut so pay is easy to add up. A booked client who does not come is set to
No-show
. After two, ask them to book with a card or come in as a walk-in.
Cuts this week, no-shows and payments.
Not yet marked
My cuts
Failed payments
Walk-ins vs bookings
Chair rent due or late
Walk-ins are the life of a barbershop and the biggest source of lost money: a client who sees a 90-minute wait and walks out is gone. A fair, visible queue keeps them in the chair.
Running the queue
Every walk-in gets added at the door as a cut with
How they came in
set to Walk-in, and the barber they want, or "next available."
Tell them an honest wait. Count the people ahead and the cuts in progress: a fade is 40 to 45 minutes, a line-up 15.
Offer a text when they are two away, so they can grab a coffee instead of leaving.
Booked clients keep their time. Walk-ins fill the gaps between bookings.
When the client sits down, write how long they waited in
Waited (minutes)
Rush hours

Friday afternoons and Saturday mornings are the rush. Put every barber on the floor, keep the apprentice on line-ups and kids cuts, and push regulars toward booked times on quieter days: "Tuesdays at 11 you would walk straight in."
The chair checklist between clients
Clippers cleaned and disinfected, guards in the jar
Fresh neck strip and cape
Hair swept from the chair and the floor around it
Ask the next client how they want it, even regulars; check
How they like it
Example

On a Saturday at 10 am three walk-ins arrive while two barbers are on bookings. The front desk adds them, quotes 35 minutes and offers a text. One goes next door for breakfast and comes back on the text. All three are cut by 11:15; average wait 32 minutes. The Dashboard shows how many cuts were walk-ins that week.
Watching the numbers
Look at the share of walk-ins and the average wait every month. Long waits with a rising walk-in share mean it is time for another barber on Saturdays, not a longer queue.
Memberships
Members are booked or walk in like anyone else, with
How they came in
set to Member and no price on the cut: their monthly payment covers it. A member who comes in less than twice a month will usually cancel; the barber should invite them back.
Most shops mix two pay models. Commission barbers share each cut with the shop; renters pay a fixed weekly rent and keep what they cut. Both work, as long as the money is tracked every week.
Commission barbers
The shop sets the price and provides products, tools and the booking system.
The barber earns a percentage of each cut, commonly 40 to 60 percent, and keeps their tips.
Pay is worked out from the Cuts table: filter by barber and the pay period, add up the price column, apply the percentage, add tips.
Chair renters
The renter pays a fixed weekly rent, sets their own prices within the shop's range, and keeps all cut income and tips.
Each week gets a row in
Chair rent
with the amount and
Due
status.
Paid on Monday: set
Paid
and the date. Not paid by Wednesday: set
Late
and talk to the barber that day.
Which model, for whom
Newer barbers usually do better on commission while they build a book. A barber with a full book of regulars often prefers rent. Write the agreement down and review it every six months.
Weekly money checklist
Every cut marked done with price and tip
Commission worked out for each commission barber
Chair rent for the week marked Paid, Due or Late
Card and cash totals match the payments list
Member payments that failed are followed up
Example

Thaddeus rents his chair for $225 a week; Dario works on 50 percent commission. On Monday the owner marks Thaddeus's rent Paid, then filters last week's cuts to Dario: $1,640 of cuts, so $820 commission plus $210 in tips. Elodie's rent from last week shows Late; the owner asks her about it before lunch.
Late rent
One late week is a conversation. Two in a row means a written plan with dates. Never take it out of a client payment without the barber agreeing in writing.
Clean tools are the law and the first thing clients notice. Every barber follows the same routine, every client, every day.
Between every client
Brush hair off clippers and trimmers, spray with disinfectant, let it sit for the time on the label
Combs and guards into the disinfectant jar for the full contact time
New neck strip; cape that touches skin is changed or wiped
Single-use razor blade for every shave and line-up; blade into the sharps box
Wash hands
Every morning
Fresh disinfectant in the jars, mixed to the label
Towels clean and stored in a closed cabinet
Hot towel cabinet cleaned and at temperature
Stations wiped: chair, armrests, counter, mirror
Every night
Floors swept and mopped, hair bagged and out
Clippers oiled, blades checked for chips
Sharps box checked; swapped when it is three-quarters full
Dirty towels and capes in the wash
Cuts and nicks

Stop, apply pressure with clean gauze, use a styptic, and never touch blood with bare hands. Throw away the blade and anything that touched blood. Write it down if the client needed more than a minute of care.
Skin conditions
If a client has an open sore, rash or sign of infection on the area you would cut, do not cut that area. Be kind, explain why, and offer to rebook.
Inspections

Keep the disinfectant label, your license and the shop license where an inspector can see them. The owner walks the stations once a week with this checklist; anything missed is a five-minute talk at the next team meeting.
Example
An inspector visits on a Thursday. Every jar is fresh, blades are single-use and the sharps box is half full. The only note is a towel cabinet left open; it is fixed on the spot.
New barbers and apprentices shadow this routine for their first week, then the owner watches them do it alone before they take clients on their own.
